summary:
Zambia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is actively enforced. Amnesty International's campaign of 26 November 2024, "Madalitso's story", follows a 36-year-old Zambian medical professional who had served three years of his sentence by November 2024 for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of workers. The case is presented by Amnesty as illustrative of the persecution of LGBTI people in the country.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, together with prolonged detentions, and advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTI individuals, with on-the-spot fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha, roughly $30 to $900. The 2022 report adds that officers who detain LGBTQI+ members often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release. LGBTQI+ people also face societal violence driven by prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of the law.

Forced anal examinations have been used to gather evidence in same-sex conduct prosecutions. Human Rights Watch's 2016 report "Dignity Debased" documents the practice in at least eight countries including Zambia, where it is less frequent than in Egypt and Tunisia but where prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal examinations as court evidence, including in a mass trial of about 20 men. Victims treat such examinations as painful, degrading sexual violence; Amnesty International described a 2014 case as tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid, and the WHO and medical authorities have condemned the practice.

Public advocacy of LGBTQ rights is effectively barred. The US State Department's 2021 report concluded that freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent, and the government does not permit advocacy of LGBTQ rights. In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalisation on a television talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court held that he was reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression, with the High Court rejecting the soliciting, public place and immoral purposes charges, though the government contested the decision.

Official policy is hostile. The 2022 country report found no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons, and while it recorded no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, a 30 May statement by President Hichilema opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults.

Violence from the public is documented and can be communal. In May 2014 residents of Marapodi in Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Threats, stalking, vandalism and hate crimes including murders are reported with little recourse to police, and most LGBTQ people in Zambia remain closeted out of fear of targeting, with lesbians described as especially vulnerable within the country's patriarchal structure.

Discrimination in employment, housing, education and health care is documented, and there are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care. The 2021 report records LGBTQI+ persons facing an inability to access healthcare services, and societal discrimination in access to health care and education is reported by the US State Department and by Global Rights/IGLHRC.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is overwhelmingly negative and organised opposition exists. A 2010 survey found that 2 percent of Zambians regard homosexuality as morally acceptable, nine points below the 11 percent recorded in neighbouring Uganda, and social attitudes are coloured by perceptions that homosexuality is immoral and a form of insanity, reflecting evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes. The NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts (ZAPASA) was formed in 1999 explicitly to combat homosexuality.

Attitudes among younger generations are reported as slightly more positive and open-minded, driven by internet access and the country's rapid digitisation exposing people to more stories from different facets of life. A statement in 2013 by Christine Kaseba, wife of then-President Michael Sata, that silence around men who have sex with men should end and that no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation, indicates that senior figures have at times broken with the official line.

The scale of the health system matters to any visitor who might need care: adult HIV prevalence stood at about 17 percent as of 2007, and the imprisonment of a trained medical professional such as Madalitso compounds an existing shortage of health workers.
localsOnly:
Section 158(3) of the penal code, amended in 2005, targets children who commit gross indecency with another child of the same sex, in public or private, or who attempt to procure such acts, making them liable to such community service or counselling as the court may determine in the best interests of the child. There is no parallel offence for minors of the opposite sex, and the provision applies only to same-sex conduct between minors.

Residents have limited formal protections in health care. The Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management based on sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy (2015) recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human.

As of July 2007 no public or private programmes provided HIV-related counselling to homosexual men, and the government National AIDS Control Program does not address same-sex relationships. The 2021 State Department report notes that LGBTQI+ persons faced an inability to access healthcare services, and societal discrimination in access to health care and education is documented by the US State Department (2010) and Global Rights/IGLHRC.

The Kasonkomona judgment remains the clearest judicial statement on advocacy: the Magistrate Court and the High Court both held that calling for decriminalisation on television was a reasonable exercise of freedom of expression, though the government contested the decision and the Registrar of Societies has stated that no LGBTQ organisation would be registered.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, or entry and visa screening for trans travellers, so those questions remain unresolved here rather than answered in the negative.

There is no information on trans-specific healthcare or medication in Zambia, including whether hormone therapy is available, restricted or obtainable privately.

Whether forced anal examinations continue to be ordered in current prosecutions is not established by these sources; the Human Rights Watch documentation dates from 2016 and the Amnesty reference from 2014, and no later case is cited.

It is unresolved whether the Kasonkomona precedent has been applied in subsequent prosecutions of advocacy, and whether the 2022 report's finding of no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws still holds in the most recent reporting year, as no post-2022 government report appears in the inventory.

Figures on HIV counselling provision and prevalence are drawn from 2007 and 2010 reporting and may not reflect current service coverage.
